newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan urges hands-off policy towards Afghan crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan urges hands-off policy towards Afghan crisis.

text.p: Kazakhstan President Nursultan Nazarbayev, speaking ahead of a special summit of five former Soviet republics, urged other states on Friday not to interfere in the internal affairs of war-battered Afghanistan.

Nazarbayev, who spoke hours before the meeting called to mull steps to prevent Afghan fighting from spilling over to Central Asian members the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), said he was ready to offer own peace initiative.
"Unfortunately the interests of many great states are focused there (in Afghanistan)," he said. "Now what is important is not to meddle in the internal affairs."

Mainly Pushtun-speaking radicals of the Taleban militia seized the Afghan capital Kabul last week and their advance north towards CIS borders, some of which are guarded with Russian help, has worried Moscow and some other regional states.

Leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and two of Afghanistan's neighbours -- Tajikistan and Uzbekistan -- will join Russia at the summit, which opens in Almaty late on Friday and should be over by early Saturday.
Moscow and others in the Commonwealth of Independent States have kept tight-lipped about how they could improve security.
But Nazarbayev said only his country was in a position to offer a proper peace proposal for Afghanistan.

"I think Kazakhstan is well-positioned to do this as Russia an some other states are not correctly perceived here," he said in a clear reference to ill-fated Moscow incursion in Afghanistan in 1979-1989.
Uzbekistan and Tajikistan are keen to separate northern clans Afghan clans locked together with southern Pushtun tribes in a prolonged power struggle.
Moscow regards the southern flank of the CIS as its strategic underbelly and Russian border guards patrol Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan.
The Afghan border has become an effective front line in a prolonged conflict between the pro-Moscow Tajik government in Dushanbe and Islamic guerrillas based in Afghanistan.
"We are following developments closely," General Andrei Nikolayev, head of the Russian border guards, told Russian Public Television on Thursday.
"I think a proposal will be worked out at this meeting that will ensure our common security in the region," he added.
Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's outspoken national security adviser, has demanded Russian action in Afghanistan.
Lebed, whose harsh statements on foreign policy have caused the Kremlin headaches in the past, said Russia should give the Afghan government forced out of Kabul all necesary help.
Foreign Minister Primakov has poured cold water on Lebed's plans. "We are a long way from sympathising with the Taleben movement, that's clear," he said on Thursday. "But I think we should wait."

Some Russian political experts have suggested Moscow should combine reinforcing guards at the border with helping warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek who controls northern Afghanistan.
But most top Moscow officials, haunted by the memory of their ill-fated intervention in Afghanistan, appear extremely cautious about helping any of the parties in the conflict.
